title: Temples of the diaspora
hookLine: immigrant temples as homes far from home

cards: A house on an ordinary street, in a city far from Asia. Shoes are piled by the front door. Inside, the living room has become a shrine room, and the kitchen smells of rice and curry.
Children in the back room are learning letters their grandparents grew up with. After a week of hard and hopeful ground, a quieter scene: the temples people built when they moved far from home.

teach.h: A RENTED ROOM, A HOUSE, A MONK INVITED.
teach.b: When families from Sri Lanka, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Tibet, Korea, Japan and elsewhere settled in new countries, some built temples, often starting small. A rented room. A house.
A building that used to be something else. Sometimes a monk was invited from home to live there.

teach.h: MORE THAN A PLACE TO SIT.
teach.b: And the temple quickly became more than a place to sit.
It's where a festival is kept on the right moon, where a child learns the chants and the old language, where a newborn is blessed, a wedding honored, and a funeral held in a way that feels right.
It's where a newcomer finds someone who knows how to fill out the forms.

The Sigalovada Sutta lays out what a lay follower and the renunciants he supports, monks among them, owe each other, in paraphrase: lay people keep their doors open and offer what renunciants need; renunciants teach, steer people from harm, and show the way.
In a diaspora temple that old exchange is easy to see. The community feeds the monk, and the monk helps hold the community together. These temples carry real strains too.
Children grow up speaking a different language than their elders. Some temples offer one service in the old language and a meditation class in English, and the two groups don't always meet.
Some communities are working on that, and some aren't yet.

teach.h: TRUST IS THE BEST OF RELATIONSHIPS.
teach.b: An old line in the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, fits these places: "trust is the best of relationships." A temple far from home runs on trust, and it builds it too.

how: Some Buddhist communities who have moved abroad have built temples, from rented rooms to large buildings, where they keep festivals, teach children the chants and language, support resident monastics and welcome newcomers.

games.why: some temples began small, in rented rooms and houses, and grew into places that hold a whole community.

practice: Remember a time you were the new one, a new school, a new job, a new country, and who made it a little easier, and let that memory stay a moment.
Then bring to mind someone new near you now, a neighbor, a coworker, a family at your children's school, and picture one small welcome: a name learned, a tip about the town, a plate of food.

wordCard.voice: Vihara. A dwelling, and so a temple, built by people who moved far from home, where the chants, the festivals, the old language and the community are kept alive. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali vihara: a dwelling, and so a monastery or temple, a place to live as much as to sit.

carryVoice: Your line: a home far from home. Shoes by the door, and a whole community inside. Rest well.
